title: AI's Real Value Is Upstream
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell argues that CEOs are looking for AI returns in the wrong place. Most companies apply AI downstream, helping employees draft emails and summarize meetings, while the larger opportunity is upstream in the CEO's own strategic work of setting direction, allocating resources and making decisions. For AI to help there, it must understand how the company actually operates, and many CEOs have never written that down. He revives his long-standing advice to make the implicit explicit and warns against leadership by ESP, where people guess what the CEO means. He lists five things an AI system needs to know: where the company is going, who is responsible for what, who can decide what, what matters right now, and how the company keeps itself on track. The piece ends with a test, whether a new executive could be handed documents explaining all five, and a plug for his firm's onboarding program.
points: AI initiatives disappoint because they target individual tasks downstream instead of the CEO's strategic decisions, which is the difference between doing more stuff and doing more of the right stuff.
Pointing AI at a company with fuzzy priorities and remade decisions produces more disorder at greater speed, so management clarity has to come first.
Leadership by ESP, where the CEO communicates something broad and others infer it, is a poor way to manage people and a worse foundation for AI.
The five things an AI must know are strategy, ownership of outcomes, decision rights, current quarterly goals and the company's management rhythms.
A simple test is whether a capable new executive could be handed documents covering strategy, responsibilities, decision rights, goals and operating rhythms.
quotes: But the much bigger opportunity is upstream, in the CEO’s strategic work: setting direction, allocating resources, making decisions, and keeping the organization focused on its goals.
It’s the difference between doing more stuff, and doing more of the right stuff.

But if you point it at a company where priorities live in the CEO’s head, accountability is fuzzy, and decisions get remade every week, it will produce more disorder at greater speed and with more confidence.
I call this leadership by ESP. The CEO communicates something broad, people try to infer the intended meaning, and the organization moves forward based on a collection of educated guesses.
The better your people are, the less you need to dictate their methods. But you still need to give them clear objectives, appropriate authority, and enough context to make good decisions.

Compare that with simply asking the department to find ways to use AI. You will probably get plenty of ideas and experiments, but it will be difficult to know whether any of them are making a meaningful difference.
If those documents do not exist, creating them may be the most valuable thing you can do to prepare your company for AI.
